---
title: Why I Keep a Workshop
date: March 3, 2026
description: Notes on wood, tools and patience
---

Building this workshop over the past few years has been the project of a lifetime.

I sanded, glued and fixed one thing after another but never stopped to ask myself **why I keep at it**.

Why do I get up before sunrise to sweep the sawdust?  
Why do I fuss over the grain of every board?  
Why do I sharpen chisels that are already sharp?

The reason, my reason, is what I hope to set down here.

## Why Not

A quick answer is "why not." Just cut, just join, just finish, and then one day look up and count the chairs you have made.

If I built a table, wouldn't I care if it was oak or pine? Wouldn't I care if it stood on a stone floor or a soft rug? Wouldn't I care if people wanted to sit at it or not?

A careless cut is a wasted board.

Planing one edge can be structural or decorative. **The intent matters**.

Even in the dull parts of the work, there is intent if we care to look.

## The Joiner

The old man who sold me my first bench was a joiner. I spent a few winters helping him move lumber, fit drawers and patch window frames.

It seemed like no matter how much we did, there was always another frame to patch. The moment one drawer slid well, the next one stuck. This cycle not only repeated while I was there but was the shape of the many years he kept that shop open.

I often wondered why he kept going. Was it the money? Was it habit?

I never asked him, but I do know what would happen if he stopped.

The frames would warp, the drawers would jam, and the damp would get into everything.

But this isn't only true of a shop.

Don't we all start the day with more to fix than a day can hold?  
Don't we all repair a thing knowing it will need repair again?  
Don't we all feel the pull between the quick fix and the careful one?

**Joiners are keepers**, holding things together that would otherwise come apart. Season after season, they square the same door and plane the same sill so that a house stays warm, dry and pleasant to live in.

This patient care, turning loose parts into something that holds, is very meaningful to me.

**I am a joiner.**

### The Teacher

I don't like noise. I wince at a dropped hammer on concrete or a router started without warning in a quiet room.

But even though I don't like loud rooms, I'm drawn to the busy mess of a class full of beginners making their first cuts.

**Beginners are wonderfully unpredictable.**

They can hold two ideas at once, like being afraid of the saw and thrilled to use it, or doubting their hands while laughing at their first crooked joint.

They are also shaped by small moments, like the smell of fresh pine or a single kind word after a ruined board.

I believe this early stage must be protected and encouraged.

I love the picture of a patient teacher. While the students are lost in their own pieces, wondering which clamp to use and where to put the glue, the teacher is watching, handing over tools, and nudging.

This teaching habit also shapes how I work alone. It means leaving notes for the next person, not just finishing the piece. It means slowing down when someone asks a question in the middle of a busy afternoon.

Helping someone make their first good joint is a real privilege.

**I am a teacher.**

### The Tinkerer

My first radio was a hand-me-down with a cracked case. It didn't work.

My cousin had replaced it and left it behind. I was too young to care about the news, so I just kept it on a shelf as if it were a prize.

One day I wanted to know what was inside. How did it pick up voices from the air? I unscrewed the back and lifted out every part I could: a speaker, a dial, a circuit board, a coil of wire.

After looking at each part for maybe an hour, I decided the only thing left was to put it back together. Several tries failed, and I started to worry.

Then something wonderful happened... The radio crackled and played!

That cycle of taking apart, looking closely, and putting back was a thrill, but what made me proudest was carrying a radio that I knew how to open and close again. I knew how it worked. How great was that!

Owning a working thing wasn't enough; I wanted to know why it worked. That also made something clear: I'm more of a tinkerer than a maker.

A **maker** wants to produce, ship, deliver.

A **tinkerer** wants to open, adjust, improve.

I love taking tools so plain nobody bothers to understand them and learning them inside out. I love finding the machine that hums a little wrong and tracing it to one loose screw.

**I am a tinkerer.**

## The Shop

So where does all of that leave me? Why am I in the shop today?

When a friend offered me his empty garage, my first thought was "Why not?"

For that moment, this was enough. Now, years later, what keeps me sweeping the floor?

Here it is. My short list. My reason.

**To keep a place where good things get made slowly.**

As a **joiner**... I'm watching the wood, the humidity, the seasons. Everything from a wet spring to a dry winter could change what I'm building. Sometimes this means checking every board in the rack to see which ones moved. It could also mean buying better clamps to make the next year easier. **Being a joiner always means caring for what comes next.**

As a **teacher**... I'm close to the people who come through the door. A teacher should have sawdust on the same sleeves and stop the whole class for the one student who is stuck. Sometimes this means showing a cut three times. Other times it means writing down a safer way to use the table saw. **Being a teacher always means being patient and careful.**

As a **tinkerer**... I'm learning the basics and taking the mystery out of them. Behind every habit is a reason; behind every squeak is a loose part. Sometimes this means building a jig to save hours of work. Other times it means trying a new tool until it feels familiar. **Being a tinkerer always means being curious and open.**

That's why I keep a workshop.
